title: Identification of Compounds and Gases - Advanced
subject: Combined Science (Chemistry)
constraints: No flame tests; no bromide; no concentrated NH₃; no lead compounds; no H₂S; no K₂Cr₂O₇

questions.question: A colourless gas is produced when dilute HCl is added to a white solid. The gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. The gas is:
questions.explanation: A gas that forms a white precipitate with limewater is carbon dioxide (CO₂). The white precipitate formed is calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).

questions.question: A colourless gas with a pungent smell is released when a white solid is warmed with NaOH solution. The gas turns moist red litmus paper blue. The gas is:
questions.explanation: A pungent gas that turns moist red litmus paper blue is ammonia (NH₃). This confirms the presence of ammonium ions (NH₄⁺) in the original solid.

questions.question: A colourless gas is produced when a metal is added to dilute sulfuric acid. The gas extinguishes a burning splint with a 'pop' sound. The gas is:
questions.explanation: A gas that extinguishes a burning splint with a 'pop' sound is hydrogen (H₂). This is produced when reactive metals react with dilute acids.

questions.question: A colourless gas relights a glowing splint. The gas is:
questions.explanation: A gas that relights a glowing splint is oxygen (O₂). This is the standard test for oxygen.

questions.question: A greenish-yellow gas with a pungent choking smell is produced. The gas bleaches moist blue litmus paper, turning it white. The gas is:
questions.explanation: A greenish-yellow gas that bleaches moist litmus paper (turns it white) is chlorine (Cl₂). Chlorine is a bleaching agent.

questions.question: A white solid produces effervescence when dilute HCl is added. The gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. The remaining solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH that is insoluble in excess. The solid is:
questions.explanation: Gas forming white precipitate with limewater indicates CO₂, confirming CO₃²⁻. White precipitate with NaOH insoluble in excess indicates Ca²⁺. Thus, CaCO₃.

questions.question: A white solid gives a pungent gas when warmed with NaOH. The gas turns moist red litmus blue. The solid dissolved in water gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. The solid is:
questions.explanation: Pungent gas turning moist red litmus blue is NH₃, confirming NH₄⁺. White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ indicates SO₄²⁻. Thus, (NH₄)₂SO₄.

questions.question: Zinc metal is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. A gas is evolved. Which statement about the gas is correct?
options: It forms a white precipitate with limewater
It turns moist red litmus blue
questions.explanation: Zinc reacts with dilute HCl to produce hydrogen gas (Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂). Hydrogen burns with a 'pop' sound when a lighted splint is applied.

questions.question: A brown gas is observed when a solid nitrate is heated strongly. The brown gas is:
questions.explanation: When most nitrates (except Group I nitrates) are heated, they decompose to produce brown nitrogen dioxide gas (NO₂) and oxygen.

questions.question: When copper(II) nitrate is heated strongly, the gases produced are:
questions.explanation: Copper(II) nitrate decomposes on heating: 2Cu(NO₃)₂ → 2CuO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Brown NO₂ gas and colourless O₂ (relights glowing splint) are produced.

questions.question: A solid compound is heated. A brown gas and a colourless gas are evolved. The colourless gas relights a glowing splint. The residue is a black solid that turns blue when water is added. The original compound is:
questions.explanation: Brown gas (NO₂) and colourless gas relighting glowing splint (O₂) indicate thermal decomposition of a nitrate. Black residue turning blue with water indicates CuO (anhydrous copper(II) oxide turns blue when hydrated). Thus, Cu(NO₃)₂.

questions.question: Solid X produces a gas when heated. The gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. The residue dissolves in dilute HCl to give a solution that produces a white precipitate with NaOH, insoluble in excess. Solid X is:
questions.explanation: Gas forming white precipitate with limewater is CO₂, indicating carbonate decomposition. Residue is the metal oxide. Dissolving in HCl and testing with NaOH gives white precipitate insoluble in excess, indicating Ca²⁺. Thus, CaCO₃ (decomposes to CaO + CO₂).

questions.question: A pale green solution gives a dirty green precipitate with NaOH that turns reddish-brown on standing. When magnesium ribbon is added to the original solution, a gas is evolved that burns with a 'pop' sound. The solution contains:
questions.explanation: Dirty green precipitate with NaOH turning reddish-brown indicates Fe²⁺ (Fe(OH)₂ oxidises to Fe(OH)₃). Magnesium reacting to produce H₂ (pop sound) confirms an acidic solution. Thus, Fe²⁺ ions.

questions.question: An unknown gas turns moist blue litmus paper red, then bleaches it white. The gas is:
questions.explanation: A gas that first turns moist blue litmus red (acidic) then bleaches it white is chlorine (Cl₂). Chlorine dissolves in water to form acids, then acts as a bleaching agent.

questions.question: A blue solution gives a blue precipitate with NaOH that is insoluble in excess. When zinc metal is added to the solution, a gas is evolved that burns with a 'pop' sound, and a reddish-brown solid deposits on the zinc. The solution contains:
questions.explanation: Blue precipitate with NaOH insoluble in excess indicates Cu²⁺. Zinc displacing a metal (reddish-brown = copper) and evolving H₂ (pop sound) confirms Cu²⁺ in acidic solution. Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

questions.question: A solid is heated in a test tube. A colourless liquid collects at the cooler end of the tube. The liquid boils at 100°C and turns anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper from blue to pink. The liquid is:
questions.explanation: A colourless liquid that boils at 100°C and turns anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper from blue to pink is water (H₂O). These are the two standard tests for water.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the tests for water?
options: Boils at 0°C and turns cobalt(II) chloride paper pink
Boils at 100°C and turns cobalt(II) chloride paper blue
Boils at 100°C and turns anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper from blue to pink
Freezes at 100°C and turns cobalt(II) chloride paper pink
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C (at standard atmospheric pressure) and turns anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper from blue to pink. These are the two tests for water.

questions.question: A white solid dissolves in water to give a colourless solution. Adding dilute HCl to the solid produces effervescence and a gas that forms a white precipitate with limewater. The solution gives no precipitate with NaOH. The original solid is:
questions.explanation: Gas forming white precipitate with limewater confirms CO₃²⁻. No precipitate with NaOH indicates a Group I cation (Na⁺ or K⁺). Thus, Na₂CO₃.

questions.question: When hydrogen peroxide decomposes in the presence of manganese(IV) oxide catalyst, the gas produced:
options: Forms a white precipitate with limewater
questions.explanation: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes to produce oxygen gas: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Oxygen relights a glowing splint.

questions.question: A solid nitrate is heated strongly. A brown gas is evolved, and the residue is a reddish-brown solid. The original nitrate is:
questions.explanation: Brown gas (NO₂) indicates nitrate decomposition. Reddish-brown residue is Fe₂O₃ (iron(III) oxide). Thus, Fe(NO₃)₃. Note: Cu(NO₃)₂ gives black CuO residue.

questions.question: Gas X turns moist red litmus blue. Gas Y forms a white precipitate with limewater. Gas Z burns with a 'pop' sound. The gases X, Y, and Z are:
options: X = CO₂, Y = NH₃, Z = O₂
X = NH₃, Y = CO₂, Z = H₂
X = Cl₂, Y = SO₂, Z = H₂
X = NH₃, Y = SO₂, Z = O₂
questions.explanation: X turns moist red litmus blue → NH₃ (alkaline gas). Y forms white precipitate with limewater → CO₂. Z burns with 'pop' sound → H₂. Thus, X = NH₃, Y = CO₂, Z = H₂.

questions.question: A carbonate X is heated strongly. It does NOT decompose. When dilute HCl is added to X, effervescence occurs and the gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. The solution gives no precipitate with NaOH. X is:
questions.explanation: A carbonate that does NOT decompose on heating is a Group I carbonate (Na₂CO₃ or K₂CO₃). No precipitate with NaOH confirms Na⁺. Gas with HCl forming white precipitate with limewater confirms CO₃²⁻. Thus, Na₂CO₃.

questions.question: A student heats solid ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl). Which observation is correct?
options: The solid sublimes and white fumes are seen
A gas that relights a glowing splint is evolved
The solid melts to form a colourless liquid
questions.explanation: Ammonium chloride sublimes when heated (solid → gas directly). White fumes of NH₄Cl are observed as it decomposes and recombines: NH₄Cl → NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl (white fumes).

questions.question: A solution gives a reddish-brown precipitate with NaOH. When the solution is warmed with NaOH, no gas is evolved. The solution gives no precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. It gives a white precipitate with AgNO₃ that is soluble in dilute NH₃. The compound is:
questions.explanation: Reddish-brown precipitate with NaOH indicates Fe³⁺. No gas when warmed rules out NH₄⁺. No precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ rules out SO₄²⁻. White precipitate with AgNO₃ soluble in dilute NH₃ indicates Cl⁻. Thus, FeCl₃.

questions.question: A white solid produces two gases when heated. One gas forms a white precipitate with limewater, and the other turns moist red litmus blue. The solid is:
questions.explanation: Gas forming white precipitate with limewater is CO₂. Gas turning moist red litmus blue is NH₃. A compound releasing both CO₂ and NH₃ on heating is ammonium carbonate: (NH₄)₂CO₃ → 2NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O.

questions.question: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to potassium manganate(VII). A greenish-yellow gas with a choking smell is evolved. The gas is:
questions.explanation: Greenish-yellow gas with choking smell is chlorine (Cl₂). KMnO₄ oxidises HCl to produce Cl₂: 2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 8H₂O + 5Cl₂.

questions.question: A compound gives a yellow precipitate with AgNO₃ that is insoluble in dilute NH₃. When the compound is heated with NaOH solution, a pungent gas is evolved that turns moist red litmus blue. The compound is:
questions.explanation: Yellow precipitate with AgNO₃ insoluble in dilute NH₃ indicates I⁻. Pungent gas turning moist red litmus blue is NH₃, confirming NH₄⁺. Thus, NH₄I.

questions.question: A blue solution is electrolysed. At the cathode, a reddish-brown solid is deposited. At the anode, a greenish-yellow gas with a pungent smell is evolved. The electrolyte is:
questions.explanation: Blue solution indicates Cu²⁺. Reddish-brown solid at cathode is copper metal. Greenish-yellow gas at anode is chlorine. Thus, the electrolyte is CuCl₂(aq).

questions.question: A gas jar of chlorine is inverted over a gas jar of ammonia. The observation is:
questions.explanation: When chlorine and ammonia gases mix, they react to form white fumes of ammonium chloride: 8NH₃ + 3Cl₂ → N₂ + 6NH₄Cl. The NH₄Cl appears as white fumes/smoke.

questions.question: A gas turns moist blue litmus red but does NOT bleach it. The gas also forms a white precipitate with limewater. The gas is:
questions.explanation: A gas that turns moist blue litmus red (acidic) but does NOT bleach it, and forms a white precipitate with limewater, is carbon dioxide (CO₂). Chlorine would bleach the litmus.

questions.question: Solid sodium carbonate is heated with solid ammonium chloride. The gas evolved:
options: Forms a white precipitate with limewater
questions.explanation: When Na₂CO₃ is heated with NH₄Cl, ammonia gas is released: Na₂CO₃ + 2NH₄Cl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ + 2NH₃. The dominant gas detected is NH₃, which turns moist red litmus blue.

questions.question: An unknown compound X gives effervescence with dilute HCl. The gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. When NaOH is added to a solution of X, a white precipitate forms that dissolves in excess NaOH. Adding AgNO₃ to another portion gives no precipitate. X is:
questions.explanation: Gas forming white precipitate with limewater confirms CO₃²⁻. White precipitate with NaOH soluble in excess indicates Zn²⁺ (amphoteric). No precipitate with AgNO₃ rules out Cl⁻ and I⁻. Thus, ZnCO₃.

questions.question: A mixture of gases is tested. Gas A turns moist red litmus blue. Gas B turns moist blue litmus red and bleaches it. Gas C has no effect on litmus but relights a glowing splint. The gases A, B and C are:
options: A = NH₃, B = Cl₂, C = O₂
A = CO₂, B = Cl₂, C = H₂
A = NH₃, B = CO₂, C = O₂
A = Cl₂, B = NH₃, C = CO₂
questions.explanation: A turns moist red litmus blue → NH₃ (alkaline). B turns moist blue litmus red then bleaches it → Cl₂. C has no effect on litmus but relights glowing splint → O₂. Thus, A = NH₃, B = Cl₂, C = O₂.

questions.question: A solid is heated and a gas is evolved. The gas has no effect on limewater and does not burn with a 'pop' sound, but it relights a glowing splint. The solid could be:
questions.explanation: Gas that relights glowing splint is O₂. No effect on limewater rules out CO₂. KNO₃ (potassium nitrate, a Group I nitrate) decomposes to give O₂: 2KNO₃ → 2KNO₂ + O₂.

questions.question: A student adds dilute HCl to four different white solids W, X, Y, and Z. The observations are: W - no reaction; X - effervescence, gas forms white precipitate with limewater; Y - effervescence, gas has no effect on limewater but burns with 'pop' sound; Z - no effervescence but solid dissolves. The solids are:
options: W = NaCl, X = Na₂CO₃, Y = Mg, Z = NaOH
W = NaOH, X = Na₂CO₃, Y = Zn, Z = NaCl
W = NaCl, X = CaCO₃, Y = Zn, Z = NaOH
W = CaSO₄, X = Na₂CO₃, Y = Mg, Z = NaCl
questions.explanation: W - no reaction with HCl indicates NaCl (already a chloride). X - CO₂ evolved indicates carbonate (Na₂CO₃). Y - H₂ evolved indicates reactive metal (Mg). Z - dissolves without gas indicates base or soluble compound (NaOH neutralises HCl).

questions.question: Two colourless solutions P and Q are tested. P gives a white precipitate with AgNO₃ that is soluble in dilute NH₃. Q gives a yellow precipitate with AgNO₃ that is insoluble in dilute NH₃. The anions in P and Q are:
questions.explanation: White precipitate with AgNO₃ soluble in dilute NH₃ indicates Cl⁻ (AgCl). Yellow precipitate with AgNO₃ insoluble in dilute NH₃ indicates I⁻ (AgI). Thus, P = Cl⁻, Q = I⁻.

questions.question: A green solution is divided into two portions. Portion 1 gives a green precipitate with NaOH that turns reddish-brown on standing in air. Portion 2 gives a white precipitate with acidified BaCl₂. The solution contains:
questions.explanation: Green precipitate with NaOH turning reddish-brown in air indicates Fe²⁺ (Fe(OH)₂ oxidises to Fe(OH)₃). White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂ indicates SO₄²⁻. Thus, Fe²⁺ and SO₄²⁻.

questions.question: A student adds excess NaOH to solutions of four different cations. The results are shown: Solution A - white precipitate, insoluble in excess; Solution B - white precipitate, soluble in excess; Solution C - blue precipitate, insoluble in excess; Solution D - reddish-brown precipitate. Which solution contains Zn²⁺?
questions.explanation: Zn(OH)₂ is amphoteric - it forms a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH to form zincate ions. Solution B shows this behaviour. (A = Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺, C = Cu²⁺, D = Fe³⁺)

questions.question: Thermal decomposition of which compound produces ONLY oxygen gas?
questions.explanation: H₂O₂ decomposes to produce only O₂ and H₂O: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Cu(NO₃)₂ produces NO₂ and O₂. CaCO₃ produces CO₂. NH₄Cl sublimes to NH₃ and HCl.

questions.question: A colourless liquid is tested. It boils at 100°C and turns anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper from blue to pink. The liquid is confirmed to be:
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure and turns anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper from blue to pink. Both tests together confirm the liquid is water.

questions.question: A compound is heated and a colourless liquid condenses. The liquid freezes at 0°C and turns blue cobalt(II) chloride paper pink. Which statement is correct?
options: The liquid cannot be identified from these tests
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C. Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride (blue) turns pink when water is added. Both observations confirm the liquid is water.

questions.question: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) is heated gently. A colourless liquid collects at the cooler end of the test tube. The liquid boils at 100°C. The remaining solid is:
questions.explanation: When hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated, water is driven off (confirmed by boiling at 100°C). The blue hydrated salt becomes white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (CuSO₄).

questions.question: Which pair of tests would confirm that a colourless liquid is pure water?
options: Freezes at 10°C and turns cobalt(II) chloride paper pink
Boils at 100°C and turns blue cobalt(II) chloride paper pink
Boils at 78°C and turns cobalt(II) chloride paper pink
Turns cobalt(II) chloride paper pink and has no smell
questions.explanation: Pure water boils at exactly 100°C (at 1 atm) and turns anhydrous blue cobalt(II) chloride paper pink. Ethanol boils at 78°C, so option C is wrong. Both tests are needed to confirm pure water.

questions.question: A solid is heated strongly. Water vapour is evolved (confirmed by boiling point of 100°C and cobalt(II) chloride test). The residue turns from blue to white. Adding water to the white residue turns it blue again. The original solid is:
questions.explanation: Water vapour evolved indicates a hydrated compound. Blue solid turning white indicates loss of water of crystallisation from CuSO₄·5H₂O. White residue turning blue with water confirms anhydrous CuSO₄. Original solid is hydrated copper(II) sulfate.

questions.question: A gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. When excess of the gas is bubbled through, the white precipitate dissolves to give a colourless solution. The gas is:
questions.explanation: CO₂ forms white precipitate (CaCO₃) with limewater. Excess CO₂ dissolves the precipitate: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂ (soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate). This is characteristic of CO₂.

questions.question: A white solid gives effervescence with dilute HCl. The gas forms a white precipitate with limewater. The remaining solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH. The same solution gives a white precipitate with NH₃ that does NOT dissolve in excess NH₃. The cation present is:
questions.explanation: Gas forming white precipitate with limewater confirms CO₃²⁻. White precipitate with NaOH soluble in excess indicates Zn²⁺ or Al³⁺. White precipitate with NH₃ insoluble in excess indicates Al³⁺ (Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NH₃). Thus, Al³⁺.
